objectives: Read age × sex pyramids + classify Sundbärg expansive / stationary / regressive types.
Apply demographic-transition staging including Van de Kaa's second demographic transition.
Compare contemporary case studies — Japan, Niger, China, India.

slides.title: Age × sex structure + dependency ratios + Sundbärg types
slides.body:
A **population pyramid** plots the number (or share) of people by age + sex — males to the left, females to the right, with age increasing vertically. It is demography's single most informative summary statistic: a snapshot encoding ~100 years of fertility, mortality, migration, and historical shocks.

**Construction**:
- Single-year, 5-year, or 10-year age groups (commonly 5-year with an open-ended terminal class like 85+ or 100+).
- Counts (absolute) or shares (%); for cross-country comparison use shares.
- Width at age $a$ reflects the surviving cohort born $a$ years ago, minus net out-migration, plus net in-migration.

**Sundbärg's typology** (Gustav Sundbärg, Swedish statistician, 1900): three canonical shapes for the relative size of ages 0-14 vs 15-49 vs 50+.
- **Expansive (progressive)**: wide base, rapidly tapering — high fertility + high mortality (early-transition; modern sub-Saharan Africa; Niger 2024 has ~50% of population under 15).
- **Stationary**: rectangular up to the elderly years — low fertility ≈ replacement + low mortality (mature transition; classic 1960s Sweden; US-style 1950).
- **Regressive (constrictive)**: narrower base than middle ages + bulging at older ages — sub-replacement fertility + low mortality (post-transition; Japan, Italy, Germany, Korea, China, Italy 2023).

**Sex ratios**:
- Sex ratio at birth (SRB) ≈ 105 boys : 100 girls (biological baseline).
- Imbalances: China + India + parts of the Caucasus have elevated SRB (~110-120) reflecting sex-selective abortion (Sen 1990 *Missing Women*; Bhalotra + Cochrane); post-Soviet states had male-mortality crises (1990s Russia SRB at older ages reflects 10-year male-life-expectancy gap).
- Older-age sex ratios: female surplus reflects female advantage in mortality (biological + behavioral).

**Dependency ratios** measure the economic load of dependents per worker:
- **Total dependency ratio** = (pop < 15 + pop 65+) / pop 15-64.
- **Youth dependency ratio** = pop < 15 / pop 15-64.
- **Old-age dependency ratio (OADR)** = pop 65+ / pop 15-64.
- **Prospective old-age dependency ratio** (Sanderson + Scherbov 2008) — counts as 'old' those with remaining life expectancy < 15 years; corrects for rising healthy life expectancy.

**Demographic dividend**: as fertility falls, the working-age share rises before population aging sets in (transition stages 3-4). Bloom + Williamson (1998) attributed ~1/3 of the East Asian growth miracle (1965-1990) to this transient bulge. **Window** opens ~15-20 years after fertility transition starts + closes as the bulge ages (~50 years).

The interactive pyramid above lets you toggle country + year; try Italy 2023 vs Niger 2024 vs Japan 2050 (projected) to see Sundbärg's three types instantiated.

slides.title: Demographic transition stages 1-5 + the second demographic transition
slides.body:
**Notestein 1945** + later authors expanded the demographic transition to four or five stages:

**Stage 1 — Pre-transition / High Stationary**: CBR ~35-50; CDR ~30-40; growth ~0-0.5% with volatility (famine, plague, war). Life expectancy ~25-35; TFR ~5-7; high infant + child mortality. Pyramid: very wide base, rapid taper, low life expectancy → few elderly. (Most of human history; small remote populations today.)

**Stage 2 — Early Expanding**: CDR falls (sanitation, nutrition, public health, vaccines); CBR remains high. RNI rises to 2-3%; doubling time 25-35 years. Pyramid: wide base + growing middle. (Sub-Saharan Africa 1950-1990; South Asia 1950-1980; Latin America 1930s-1960s.)

**Stage 3 — Late Expanding**: CBR falls toward replacement; CDR continues low. RNI slows. Pyramid: narrowing base + bulging middle. (Latin America 1970s-1990s; South + Southeast Asia 1980s-2010s; sub-Saharan Africa 2000s-present, slower than predicted.)

**Stage 4 — Low Stationary**: CBR ≈ CDR ≈ 10-12; RNI ~0; TFR near replacement 2.1; life expectancy 75+. Pyramid: rectangular base-to-middle + growing top. (United States 1970s-2000s before SDT; Western Europe 1960s-1970s.)

**Stage 5 — Declining / Post-transition**: CBR < CDR; RNI < 0 (natural decrease); TFR ~1.2-1.7 (sub-replacement); aging-driven CDR rise. Pyramid: narrower base than middle + heavy elderly top. (Japan, Italy, Germany, Korea, Greece, Spain, Portugal, much of Eastern Europe today; China since ~2022.)

**The Second Demographic Transition (SDT)** — Van de Kaa *Population Bulletin* (1987) + Lesthaeghe *Population and Development Review* (1995, 2010, 2014):
- Below-replacement fertility (TFR < 2.1) becomes durable.
- Rising cohabitation + nonmarital childbearing.
- Rising divorce + family complexity.
- Delayed marriage + first birth (mean age first birth 28-32 in HICs vs 21-23 mid-20th century).
- Voluntary childlessness rises.
- Drivers: rising female education + employment; effective contraception (pill 1960 + IUD); postmaterialist + individualist + self-actualization values (Inglehart's *Modernization and Postmaterialism* 1990); secularization; welfare-state support reduces dependence on family.
- Distinguished from the *first* demographic transition (Notestein) by *motivation*: family formation in SDT is structured by lifestyle + self-fulfillment + autonomy preferences, not by economic necessity.

**Lutz low-fertility trap hypothesis** (Lutz + Skirbekk + Testa 2006): TFR below ~1.5 may stabilize at low levels via three feedback mechanisms: (1) demographic (smaller cohorts of potential parents → fewer absolute births even at constant TFR); (2) economic (declining youth labor force → less optimism + delayed family formation); (3) sociological (norms shift toward smaller families). Empirical evidence mixed: Germany + Italy + Korea + Japan persist at very low; some Northern European countries recovered modestly toward 1.7-1.9 with family-friendly policy (France, Sweden) before slipping again post-2010.

**Lowest-low fertility** (Kohler + Billari + Ortega *Population and Development Review* 2002): TFR below 1.3 — now reached by Korea (0.78 in 2022, lowest ever recorded for a national population), Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Spain, Italy, Greece, Japan (briefly), much of Eastern Europe. Drivers: housing costs, intensive parenting norms, gender inequity in unpaid work, labor-market precarity, education-employment mismatch.

slides.title: Case studies: Japan 2023 + Niger 2024 + China + India
slides.body:
**Japan 2023 — super-aged + shrinking**:
- Population: 124.5 M (2023); peaked 128 M in 2010.
- TFR: 1.20 (2023), persistently low since ~1990; **lowest-low** since 2003.
- Median age: 49.5 — highest among major countries.
- Share 65+: 29.1% — first country to surpass 28%; share 80+: 9%.
- Life expectancy: 81.5 M / 87.6 F (2023) — among highest globally.
- Net migration: small but rising (~150K / yr); historically restrictive, now relaxing for elder care + IT.
- Workforce shrinking ~1% / yr; Japanese government UN WPP medium projects 87 M by 2070, ~37% over 65.
- Pyramid: narrow base, large 50-60 cohort (echo of 1947-1949 baby boom + 1971-1974 second peak), bulging 75+ tail. Classic SDT + Stage 5.
- Policy responses: pension reform + delayed retirement age; *womenomics* (Abe); robotics + AI for elder care; selective migration; rural-urban consolidation.

**Niger 2024 — extreme youth-heavy expansive**:
- Population: 27.2 M (2024); UN WPP medium projects 65 M by 2050 + 165 M by 2100.
- TFR: 6.7 (2023) — highest national TFR in the world.
- Median age: 15.4 years.
- Share under 15: 50.0% (UN WPP).
- Life expectancy: 63 (2023, up from ~38 in 1960).
- Infant mortality: ~45 per 1000 (down from ~200 in 1960).
- Pyramid: extreme triangle — wide base, rapid taper; classic Stage 2 / early Stage 3.
- Drivers of persistent high TFR: low female schooling (~ 20% women complete secondary); pronatalist + patriarchal cultural norms; low contraceptive prevalence (~12% modern methods); high desired family size (still ~7-8 children in surveys); polygyny.
- Demographic dividend: theoretically large, contingent on rapid fertility decline + youth employment + schooling — but currently growth outpaces educational + economic capacity.

**China — one-child legacy + rapid aging**:
- Population: 1.41 B (2023); **peaked in 2022** + began absolute decline. Surpassed by India in 2023.
- TFR: 1.0 (2023, NBS) — among lowest globally.
- One-child policy (1979/1980-2015) + two-child (2016-2021) + three-child (2021-): fertility didn't rebound after policy relaxation; cohort + cultural inertia + lowest-low dynamics dominate.
- Sex ratio at birth: peaked ~120 in mid-2000s; ~108 in 2020s; ~30 million 'missing women' (Sen 1990; Bhalotra + Cochrane).
- Median age: 39.8 (2023), projected 51 by 2050.
- Share 65+: 14.9% (2023), projected 30% by 2050.
- Pyramid: deep notch at <15 (one-child legacy); large bulge at 25-50 (Cultural-Revolution + reform-era cohorts); rising elderly. Sex ratio imbalance visible at 15-30.
- Implications: shrinking labor force ~3 M / yr; pension crisis (low formal coverage, family-based norms strained); housing + urban consolidation.

**India — crossover 2023 + still expanding**:
- Population: 1.43 B (2023); surpassed China April 2023 per UN.
- TFR: 2.0 (NFHS-5 2019-2021) — at replacement; declining further.
- Median age: 28.2 — about a decade younger than China.
- Share 65+: 7%; share under 15: 25%.
- Pyramid: wider base + still-growing middle; classic Stage 3 / late-Stage 4 hybrid. Substantial heterogeneity: Kerala + Tamil Nadu at lowest-low; Bihar + Uttar Pradesh still TFR > 3.
- Demographic dividend window: open until ~2055; conditional on schooling + employment + female labor-force participation (a worrying ~25-30%, low for the development level).
- Migration: substantial internal + diaspora (~18 M abroad, largest emigrant population); remittances ~$125 B / yr (largest in world).
- Sex ratio at birth: ~110 in 2010s, declining toward biological baseline; large state-level variation.

**Other cases worth knowing**:
- **Korea**: TFR 0.78 (2022) — lowest ever for any nation; Seoul ~0.6.
- **Italy**: TFR 1.21 (2023); median age 48; depopulation in southern + rural regions.
- **Russia**: post-Soviet male-mortality crisis; war + emigration shocks; pyramid scarred by WWII deaths + 1990s mortality.
- **Germany**: TFR 1.46 (2022); recovering modestly with immigration; would shrink ~0.5%/yr absent migration.
- **Nigeria**: largest African population (~225 M in 2023); UN WPP projects ~400 M by 2050 — becoming third-largest country.
- **Brazil**: TFR fell from 6.2 (1960) to 1.6 (2022) — one of the fastest transitions on record.

Lessons 3-5 develop fertility, mortality, and migration respectively; lesson 6 develops projection.

question.question: Reading three population pyramids — Niger, China, Japan
question.goal: Diagnose each country's transition stage + dominant demographic forces from its 2023 age × sex pyramid.

steps.prompt: Niger 2024 pyramid: ~50% under 15, narrow top, mean age 15.4. Stage + Sundbärg type?

acceptedAnswers: stage 2 to early stage 3, expansive Sundbärg type, high fertility and falling mortality

steps.reveal: Niger 2024 sits at Stage 2 (early-expanding) bordering Stage 3. Sundbärg **expansive** type: extreme triangle. TFR ~6.7 (highest globally); under-15 share ~50%. Life expectancy ~63 (up from ~38 in 1960) — mortality has fallen substantially; fertility transition has lagged by 30-50 years compared with mortality. Pyramid implies (a) labor force will grow rapidly through 2070; (b) need for schooling + jobs is enormous; (c) demographic dividend is theoretically large but conditional on rapid fertility decline + investment in human capital + female schooling + contraceptive access.

steps.prompt: China 2023 pyramid: notch at <15, bulge at 25-50, growing top, SRB elevated 1990-2010. Stage + dominant force?

acceptedAnswers: stage 5 post-transition, regressive Sundbärg, one-child policy legacy and rapid aging

steps.reveal: China 2023 is **Stage 5** (post-transition + decline). Sundbärg **regressive**. TFR ~1.0 (lowest-low); first absolute decline 2022. Pyramid scars: (a) one-child notch in <15 cohorts; (b) bulge 25-50 reflects reform-era youth + delayed fertility decline; (c) elderly top growing rapidly with rising life expectancy ~78. Elevated SRB (peaked ~120 mid-2000s) visible as male surplus at 15-30 — ~30 M 'missing women'. Pension + labor + marriage-market consequences playing out now. Lutz low-fertility trap looks plausible — policy relaxation (2016 → 2021 → 2024) hasn't reversed.

steps.prompt: Japan 2023 pyramid: median age 49.5, 29% over 65, narrow base. Stage + drivers?

acceptedAnswers: stage 5, regressive, second demographic transition, ultra-low fertility and very low mortality

steps.reveal: Japan 2023 is the canonical **Stage 5 / super-aged** society — first country past 28% share 65+. Sundbärg **regressive**. TFR ~1.20 since ~1990; near-stagnant net migration (until very recent rises); extreme life expectancy (81.5 M / 87.6 F). Classic **Second Demographic Transition** (Van de Kaa 1987; Lesthaeghe 1995): delayed marriage, low cohabitation but rising, high voluntary childlessness, strong gender-equity gap in unpaid work + workplace norms. Workforce shrinks ~1%/yr; pension + elder-care system stressed; rural depopulation; policy responses (womenomics, robotics, selective migration) help at margins.

steps.prompt: India 2023: TFR ~2.0, median age 28, surpassed China in population. Stage + window?

acceptedAnswers: late stage 3 to early stage 4, demographic dividend window open until 2050s, heterogeneous by state

steps.reveal: India 2023 is late Stage 3 to early Stage 4 nationally — TFR at replacement, median age 28. **Demographic dividend window** open through ~2055. Heterogeneity is the dominant fact: Kerala + Tamil Nadu at TFR ~1.5 (lowest-low SDT-style); Bihar + UP TFR > 3; net result averages to ~2.0. Crossover with China (2023) made India most populous. Critical variables: female labor-force participation (~25-30%, anomalously low for development level); youth employment; schooling; rural-urban transition; internal migration. Dividend not automatic — conditional on policy + investment.

question.question: Why is the 'demographic dividend' a transient phenomenon rather than a permanent feature of low-fertility countries?
options: The demographic dividend (Bloom + Williamson *World Bank Economic Review* 1998) is the temporary boost to economic growth that occurs when fertility decline reduces the youth-dependency share *before* aging raises the old-age-dependency share. As the fertility transition begins, child cohorts shrink while the previously-large cohorts move into prime working ages (15-64), so the working-age share peaks for ~30-50 years. Bloom + Williamson attributed ~1/3 of the East Asian growth miracle (1965-1990) to this transient bulge interacting with policy (schooling, openness, savings). But the bulge inevitably ages: the same large cohorts become the elderly 40-50 years later, raising OADR + reversing the dividend. Korea + China + Thailand are now passing through this transition. The window is open ~15-20 years after fertility decline starts + closes ~50 years later when the bulge enters retirement. Realization is *conditional* — requires investment in human capital, openness, savings, and female labor-force participation; Latin America largely missed it; East Asia + parts of Southeast Asia captured it; sub-Saharan Africa's window is opening + outcomes are not predetermined.
question.explanation: Demographic dividend (Bloom + Williamson 1998) is transient because the same cohorts that swell the working-age share later age into the elderly population. Window ~15-20 years after fertility decline starts + closes ~50 years later. Realization is conditional on schooling + labor-market policy + savings + female labor-force participation.

hints: Where does the boost come from?
What happens to the cohorts later?
slides.workedSolution: Demographic dividend = temporary rise in working-age share between youth-dependency fall + old-age-dependency rise. Bloom + Williamson (1998) explained ~1/3 of East Asian growth. Transient because the working-age bulge becomes the elderly bulge 40-50 years later. Conditional on schooling + savings + employment + openness.

question.question: Diagnosing a Korean-style lowest-low pyramid
question.prompt: Korea's TFR is 0.78 (2022) — lowest ever recorded for any national population; Seoul ~0.6. The pyramid shows a narrow base (<15) plus heavy 50-60 cohort (echo of 1955-1965 baby boom), a 25-45 hollow already forming, and rapidly growing elderly. In ≤200 words, write a diagnostic note covering: (a) which Sundbärg type + transition stage applies; (b) whether the **Lutz low-fertility trap** is operating + what evidence would discriminate; (c) which Van de Kaa second-demographic-transition dynamics (cohabitation, delayed marriage, childlessness, gender equity) are most likely contributing; (d) two policy levers + their likely effect sizes (cite France + Sweden experience). Name two datasets you'd consult (KOSTAT, Korea Labor + Income Panel Study, OECD Family Database).

question.question: A country has 200000 people under 15, 800000 aged 15-64, and 250000 aged 65+. Compute the total dependency ratio per 100 working-age.
question.hint: TDR = (pop < 15 + pop 65+) / pop 15-64 × 100. $(200000 + 250000) / 800000 \times 100 = 56.25$ — i.e. ~56 dependents per 100 workers. Youth-dependency: 25; old-age-dependency: 31.25. A maturing transition shifts mass from youth to old-age dependency.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain how to read a population pyramid + diagnose a country's transition stage. Cover Sundbärg's three types, the four (or five) Notestein stages, the second demographic transition (Van de Kaa + Lesthaeghe), and at least two contemporary case studies.
question.rubric: Mentions: pyramid = age × sex; Sundbärg expansive / stationary / regressive; Notestein stages 1 (pre-transition) → 2 (mortality fall, expansive) → 3 (fertility fall) → 4 (low stationary) → 5 (post-transition, decline). Van de Kaa + Lesthaeghe **second demographic transition** = below-replacement + cohabitation + delayed marriage + voluntary childlessness + postmaterialist values. **Lutz low-fertility trap** hypothesis for TFR < 1.5. Cases: Niger (Stage 2, expansive, TFR 6.7), Japan (Stage 5, regressive, TFR 1.2, super-aged), China (Stage 5, regressive, one-child legacy + aging, TFR 1.0, SRB scar), India (late 3 / early 4, dividend window). Dependency ratios (youth, old-age, prospective Sanderson-Scherbov). Concludes: pyramid encodes ~100 yr of fertility + mortality + migration + historical shocks; diagnosis blends shape + level of vital rates + cohort scars + policy context.
